F=ma Problem Series
Lesson 6: Data Analysis
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:31:22 t V
This week, we'll focus on error analysis and uncertainty, including error propagation.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:31:29 t V
Although this topic often appears on the F=ma exam, it's new to a lot of students in this course.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:31:38 t V
We'll learn from scratch today instead of assuming you know the basics already. That means we'll have fewer problems and more explanation today than normal.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:31:45 t V
However, 90 minutes is a short time, so it will still be pretty fast-paced.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:31:50 t V
Finally, we won't do precise derivations of the rules of error analysis today. Instead, we'll present them and try to give some of the intuition behind them so you can use them on the F=ma exam. (However, if you take PhysicsWOOT, you'll derive the rules there.)
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:32:21 t V
I put two good references on the message board concerning this topic.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:32:47 t V
Today's big idea involves thinking both intuitively and quantitatively. This means that when we solve a problem, we'll use equations and numbers, but also demand that those numbers work out to make sense. This is especially important with new topics where you haven't built much intuition yet.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:33:02 t V
Many textbooks separate their end-of-chapter problems into "conceptual" problems and "quantitative" problems. But many F=ma problems are both conceptual and quantitative, so we have to be able to use both modes of thinking when solving a problem.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:33:33 t V
I'm going to move quickly so I can cover most of the material. I know some of it will be difficult...
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:33:44 t V
Error and Uncertainty
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:33:51 t V
Suppose you use a ruler to measure the thickness of your physics textbook. You get 2.0cm.2.0cm. Is the book exactly 2.0cm2.0cm thick?

jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:34:32 t V
No, it isn't! The book might be 2.03cm2.03cm or 1.98cm1.98cm thick. The differences from 2.0cm2.0cm are so small you can't reliably measure them with just a ruler.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:34:45 t V
In fact, the book may not even have a thickness that's well-defined down to the tenth of a millimeter, since if you press on a book a bit, you may compress it and change its thickness. The book shape isn't totally uniform, either, so perhaps the center is a little thicker than the edges, for example.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:34:58 t V
In physics, when we make a measurement, that measurement is never perfect. It's a good practice to report your measurement along with its error or uncertainty. (We won't make any distinction between these two terms. As far as we're concerned, "error" and "uncertainty" mean the same thing. Neither means "mistake".)
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:35:12 t V
Suppose you use a ruler to make a measurement of 2.0cm,2.0cm, but you're uncertain about the result. Based on your experience, what might you estimate the uncertainty to be in that measurement?

jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:36:10 t V
Good estimates - for now let's take it as an assumption that you think your measurement is accurate to within 0.05cm.0.05cm. We'll return to where that number comes from in a bit. Given your uncertainty is 0.05cm,0.05cm, we write it up like this:
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:36:22 t V
x=2.0±0.05cm.x=2.0±0.05cm.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:36:27 t V
(The LaTeX for the plus-minus symbol is \pm. This will give you ±.±.)
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:36:55 t V
Also, $\mp$ changes the order.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:37:09 t V
The equation x=2.0±0.05cmx=2.0±0.05cm says that if you were to make a bunch of independent measurements, they would all be roughly 2.0cm,2.0cm, but there would be some variation, and typically the measurements would vary by about 0.05cm.0.05cm. In this case, the figure 0.05cm0.05cm is the "error" or "uncertainty" in your measurement.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:37:34 t V
However, 0.05cm0.05cm is not a hard bound for the distance from 2.0cm2.0cm to the largest or smallest possible measurement. Many of the measurements would be between 1.95cm1.95cm and 2.05cm,2.05cm, but some would still be outside that range. 0.05cm0.05cm is just the typical spread.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:37:46 t V
If we had many different people make measurements and put them in a plot, it might look like this:
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:37:48 t V
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:38:00 t V
(Actually, a computer was used to simulate one million people taking measurements. We didn't actually find one million volunteers.)
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:38:25 t V
(Computers can generate random numbers which can be used to simulate errors)
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:38:39 t V
The plot has a bell-shaped curve. This is called a Gaussian distribution and sometimes F=ma problems will mention Gaussian errors, meaning the errors come from a plot with this shape. However, we aren't worried here about the exact shape of the plot, and all the rules for error analysis that we learn today work whether we have Gaussian errors or not.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:38:58 t V
One more rule is that you should report your measurement to the same digit as your error. When we wrote ‘‘2.0cm",‘‘2.0cm", we reported it to the tenth of a centimeter, but 0.05cm,0.05cm, the error, is given in hundredths of a centimeter. So you want to report your measurement as
x=2.00±0.05cm.x=2.00±0.05cm.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:39:15 t V
We often use the symbol ΔΔ to indicate uncertainties, so we might write
Δx=0.05cm.Δx=0.05cm.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:39:19 t V
You will also sometimes see σσ used for uncertainty. In that case, you might see σx=0.05cm,σx=0.05cm, where the subscript tells us that the error is for the measurement xx.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:39:33 t V
Now let's look at our first problem in error analysis.

To distinguish error from relative error, the non-relative error is sometimes called "absolute error". However, this name won't always be used. If you see just "error" you should assume it's absolute error.

jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:50:41 t V
The relative errors coming out to be the same for time and velocity suggests that relative error follows some simple rules. Let's outline those rules.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:50:51 t V
Relative error is not changed by scaling.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:50:56 t V
This means that if you have a variable and you multiply it by some constant, the relative error doesn't change. In other words, if the relative error in xx is Δxx=0.01,Δxx=0.01, and then we define u=2x,u=2x, the relative error in uu is also 0.01.0.01.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:51:25 t V
Another way to state the same rule is:
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:51:28 t V
Scaling a variable by some factor scales the absolute error by the same factor.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:51:37 t V
For example, if u=2xu=2x and Δx=3g,Δx=3g, then Δu=6g.Δu=6g.

If we were given the error in position xx and tt was considered exact, we could interpret tt as simply scaling x.x. It would play the same role as 22 played in our previous example of u=2x.u=2x. Fortunately, there's another rule of relative error:
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 19:53:40 t V
The relative error in the reciprocal of a variable is approximately equal to the relative error in the variable, as long as the relative error is small.

For example, if Δm1Δm1 and Δm2Δm2 both have a 50/50 chance to be positive or negative, independence says that Δm2Δm2 is still split 50/50 between positive and negative even if we focus on only the times when Δm1Δm1 turns out to be positive. Summary
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 21:01:36 t V
Physical measurements all have some inherent error or uncertainty.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 21:01:44 t V
The relative error in a quantity xx is Δxx.Δxx.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 21:01:46 t V
If a variable is taken to the nnth power, its relative error is Δ(xn)xn=nΔxx.Δ(xn)xn=nΔxx.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 21:01:49 t V
If yy is a function of x,x, the error in yy is Δy=slope of y⋅Δx.Δy=slope of y⋅Δx.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 21:01:51 t V
If we have two measurements, x1x1 and x2x2 which were taken independently, the error in their sum is Δ(x1+x2)=√(Δx1)2+(Δx2)2.Δ(x1+x2)=(Δx1)2+(Δx2)2. This is called addition in quadrature and can be extended to three or more variables being summed.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 21:01:53 t V
When we multiply variables, the relative errors add in quadrature. Δ(x1x2)x1x2=√(Δx1x1)2+(Δx2x2)2.Δ(x1x2)x1x2=(Δx1x1)2+(Δx2x2)2.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 21:01:55 t V
If we have nn independent measurements of x,x, each with the same uncertainty Δx,Δx, the uncertainty in the average ¯xx¯ is Δ¯x=Δx√n.Δx¯=Δxn.
jonjoseph 2025-07-16 21:02:06 t V
**** Important Result!! ****

When different independent measurements of a certain variable have different errors, it is best not to average them, but to take a weighted average, ¯xw=αx1+(1−α)x2.x¯w=αx1+(1−α)x2. The weighted average takes more of the variable with less error. The ratio of αα to (1−α)(1−α) that minimizes the error in ¯xwx¯w obeys α1−α=(Δx2)2(Δx1)2.α1−α=(Δx2)2(Δx1)2.
